THE LAST EMPEROR OF MEXICO
A disaster in the New World 336pp. Faber. £20.
Edward Shawcross
In 1864, the Austrian archduke Maximilian invaded Mexico. He was accompanied by an ungainly crew of fanatical Mexican Catholics, Belgian mercenaries and French veterans from the bloody conquest of Algeria.

Carlotta is a beautiful naïf, sucked into this tale of silly men’s ambitions and blown out the other side an insensible wreck.
Shawcross’s research takes him beyond this standard tale. The Last Emperor of Mexico is not the author’s first book (as most reviewers have claimed). It is the second book to be based on his doctoral research, after his France, Mexico and Informal Empire in Latin America, 1820–1867 (2018), and it shows. Rooted in dozens of European archives and manuscripts, Shawcross’s argument is dotted with striking quotations from a bewildering array of Austrian courtiers, French legionaries and American hangers-on.
